title: PHP
body:
*PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor* — the server-side language [[Node.js]] is argued against in this
course. It runs on the server, embedded in the page it is producing, and it is what most of
the web's dynamic content was built in.

```php
$connection = new PDO(...);
$result1 = $connection->query(...);   // blocks until the database answers
$result2 = $connection->query(...);   // then this one blocks too
```

The line that matters: those calls are **blocking**. The thread handling that request sits
idle waiting on the database and cannot serve anyone else, so a server is sized by how many
requests it might be waiting on at once rather than by how much work it is doing. A typical
Linux server handles on the order of 2000 threads, which is why PHP sites need a lot of
servers. Node's whole pitch is that the same wait costs a callback instead of a thread; see
[[Asynchronous JS]].

That is not a verdict on the language. PHP is genuinely better at the thing it was designed
for, template-driven dynamic pages, which the course notes concede: [[Node.js]] is "not ideal
for traditional dynamic content sites". Modern PHP also runs asynchronously if you ask it to.

Other server-side environments in the same family: [[ASP.NET]] and [[Ruby on Rails]]. See
[[Server Side]] and [[Server-Side Technology]].
